stem: An elective procedure is about to begin, but no informed-consent form has been signed. The client has already received IV sedation and is now drowsy, confused, and unable to explain the procedure or its alternatives. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Ask the client to sign immediately because the procedure is already scheduled
options.B: Do not obtain a new consent signature from the client in the current state; notify the appropriate provider and follow the consent process for a client who cannot presently demonstrate decision-making capacity
options.C: Ask any available family member to sign because family presence automatically creates legal authority to consent
options.D: Proceed without consent because administration of procedural sedation creates an emergency exception

rationale: Valid informed consent requires the ability to understand relevant information, consider alternatives, and make a voluntary decision. The stem establishes that the client is currently drowsy, confused, and unable to explain the procedure or alternatives, so the nurse should not treat a new signature obtained in that state as adequate informed consent. The appropriate provider should be notified and the applicable process for decision-making incapacity and an authorized surrogate, if needed, should be followed. A family member is not automatically a legally authorized surrogate, and routine elective care does not become an emergency merely because sedation has already been administered.
educational_objective: Before relying on informed consent, verify that the client can meaningfully understand and decide; when current decision-making capacity is impaired, pause elective care and follow the appropriate provider/surrogate consent process.
source_organization: American Medical Association; National Council of State Boards of Nursing
source_document_title: AMA Code of Medical Ethics Opinion 2.1.1 — Informed Consent; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: AMA current online opinion accessed 2026-08-17; NCSBN effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31
source_locator: AMA Opinion 2.1.1: assess the patient's ability to understand relevant medical information, treatment alternatives, and make an independent voluntary decision. NCSBN Management of Care — Informed Consent, printed p.22 (PDF p.25): identify appropriate person, participate in consent, verify education and consent.
source_claim_supported: AMA identifies decision-making ability as a required element of informed consent; NCSBN defines the RN role as participating in and verifying informed consent rather than treating a signature alone as sufficient.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Management of Care — Informed Consent, printed p.22 (PDF p.25)
blueprint_topic: Management of Care — informed consent and decision-making capacity
correction_summary: Removed a vague timing rule and rebuilt the item around the clinically relevant requirement for decision-making capacity at the time consent is obtained. The stem establishes impaired capacity through behavior rather than assuming that any sedative automatically invalidates consent.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Current AMA ethics opinion and official NCSBN 2026 informed-consent content verified.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: Capacity requirement, RN verification role, and need for an authorized surrogate when capacity is absent are directly supported without asserting a universal post-sedation rule.
audit_findings.choice_A: Incorrect; the client cannot presently demonstrate capacity for informed consent.
audit_findings.choice_B: Correct; pauses elective care and invokes the appropriate consent pathway.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; family relationship alone does not automatically establish surrogate authority.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; prior sedation does not create an emergency exception for an elective procedure.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B respects both decision-making capacity and formal surrogate/provider processes.
audit_findings.cueing: All choices are realistic consent-management actions.
audit_findings.blueprint: Exact NCSBN 2026 Management of Care — Informed Consent mapping.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Checked sedative-dose assumptions, fluctuating capacity, emergency exceptions, family-surrogate law variability and scope wording; no unresolved conflict remains.
